name: Prometheus
summary: The standard open-source metrics system: it pulls numbers from your services over HTTP, stores them as labelled time series and alerts on PromQL queries.
intro: Most metrics systems wait for apps to push data to them. Prometheus does the opposite: every scrape interval (one minute by default, often set to 15 seconds) it sends an HTTP request to each target’s `/metrics` endpoint, which answers with the current values as plain text. Targets come from service discovery, such as the Kubernetes API, cloud APIs, DNS or a file, so new pods are picked up without config changes. Because Prometheus does the asking, it notices when a target stops answering: the built-in `up` series drops to 0.

Each series is a metric name plus labels, such as `http_requests_total{route="/login", status="500"}`, kept in a local time-series database on disk. You query it with PromQL, and alerting rules are PromQL expressions evaluated on a schedule; firing alerts go to the separate Alertmanager, which groups them and routes them to email, Slack or a pager. Prometheus started at SoundCloud in 2012 and graduated from the CNCF in 2018. Prometheus 3.0, released in November 2024, added a new UI, UTF-8 metric names and a built-in receiver for OpenTelemetry’s OTLP.
strengths: Service discovery finds and scrapes new targets automatically, and a dead target is visible straight away
PromQL handles rates, percentiles and label joins in one expression, and Thanos, Grafana Mimir and others speak it too
One Go binary with no external database to run
Kubernetes components and a large ecosystem of exporters already publish metrics in its text format
limits: Local storage is neither clustered nor replicated; long retention or high availability needs remote write to Thanos, Mimir or a managed service
Labels with many distinct values (user IDs, request IDs) multiply the number of series and the memory needed
Metrics only, and not exact: its own docs say not to use it for per-request billing

story: In 2012 SoundCloud was breaking its site into services: soon it had hundreds of them, with many thousands of instances started and moved around by its own in-house cluster scheduler, years before Kubernetes. Its monitoring, mostly StatsD and Graphite, had what the team later called “serious limitations”. Metrics were flat dotted names, and there was no clean way to slice them by instance, service or endpoint, or to run monitoring without a central storage backend.

Julius Volz, a former Google site reliability engineer, and Matt T. Proud, another ex-Googler, had both just joined SoundCloud. They took their inspiration from Borgmon, the system Google used to monitor services on its Borg clusters. They started building Prometheus in their free time, brought it into SoundCloud after a couple of months, and then worked on it properly on company time. SoundCloud announced it publicly in January 2015, and in May 2016 it became the second project hosted by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, after Kubernetes.

Its labelled data and pull model suited containers that come and go. Today Kubernetes components and a large ecosystem of exporters publish metrics in its text format, and long-term stores such as Thanos and Grafana Mimir answer PromQL queries.

choices.choice: Pull metrics over HTTP instead of receiving pushes
choices.why: The server asks each target for its numbers, so a missing answer immediately shows that a target is down. Anyone can also start an extra Prometheus, even on a laptop, and scrape the same targets without changing them.

choices.choice: Labels instead of dotted metric names
choices.why: SoundCloud needed to break the same metric down by instance, service, endpoint or method. Key-value labels make every dimension queryable, where a Graphite-style name fixes one hierarchy in advance.

choices.choice: One standalone server with no distributed storage
choices.why: Each server is a single binary that stores data on its own disk, so you can rely on it when the rest of your infrastructure is broken. The price is that long retention and high availability need extra systems.
Borrowed from Borgmon, which treated time-series data as the source for alerts: an alerting rule is a PromQL expression evaluated on a schedule, so the same language serves graphs and alerts.

timeline.text: Matt T. Proud and Julius Volz start Prometheus at SoundCloud

Graduates from the CNCF in August
